THOUGHT: The specimen shows a multinodular proliferation composed of numerous osteoclast‑type multinucleated giant cells admixed with mononuclear stromal cells and increased mitotic activity. CD68 positivity supports an osteoclast/histiocytic lineage for the giant cells; negativity for CD45 argues strongly against lymphoma/hematopoietic tumor, S100 and desmin negativity argue against melanocytic or myogenic lesions, and the morphology is not that of epithelial/metastatic carcinoma. The lesion is centered at the skull base/cavernous sinus/orbital apex and shows aggressive, locally destructive growth with intracranial extension — a pattern seen with primary bone tumors of the skull base. Recurrent, locally destructive behavior after repeated excisions also fits a locally aggressive primary bone lesion. The combination of osteoclast‑like giant cells plus a mononuclear stromal cell population in a young adult is most consistent with giant cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma), which can rarely arise in skull base bones (sphenoid/temporal/orbital bones) and can extend into the orbit and intracranial cavity. Other entities that can mimic this histology/imaging include giant cell–rich osteosarcoma (would show malignant osteoid on careful review), central giant cell granuloma (jaw/craniofacial variant), aneurysmal bone cyst (blood‑filled spaces and different architecture), and tenosynovial giant cell tumor/pigmented villonodular synovitis variants (usually synovial/tendon sheath distribution but can involve adjacent bone). The reported PALB2 splicing variant likely reflects a somatic DNA‑repair pathway alteration but is not specific for any of the above and does not favor a lymphoma or epithelial metastasis in this context.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Giant cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma) of the skull base/orbit — most likely given osteoclast‑like giant cells with mononuclear stromal cells, CD68 positivity, age and aggressive local bone‑centered growth with recurrence.
2. Giant cell–rich osteosarcoma (osteosarcoma with abundant osteoclast‑type giant cells) — important consideration because of increased mitoses and aggressive intracranial extension; would require demonstration of malignant osteoid to confirm.
3. Central giant cell granuloma (reparative/giant cell granuloma of craniofacial bones) — histologically similar and can occur in craniofacial bones with recurrence, but typically occurs in the jaw and in somewhat younger patients.
4. Aneurysmal bone cyst (secondary/solid variant) — can be giant‑cell rich and expansile in craniofacial bones; radiologic cystic/blood‑filled features and characteristic histologic architecture would help distinguish.
5. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (localized/intraosseous pigmented villonodular synovitis variant) — can show CD68+ giant cells and destructive behavior when arising adjacent to joints/tendon sheaths; less typical for central skull‑base bone lesions but a reasonable mimic.

Recommendation: Correlate with careful histologic search for osteoid (to exclude giant cell–rich osteosarcoma), perform H3F3A mutation testing (supports giant cell tumor of bone if positive), review radiographs for classic bone lytic/epiphyseal features, and consider multidisciplinary skull‑base tumor management.

Case Information:
A 34-year old African American woman with a history of nodular sclerosing type stage IIE Hodgkin lymphoma (treated with 4 cycles of ABVC followed by 3060 cGY at the neck and mediastinum) presented with a painless, left upper eyelid mass that had previously been excised on 3 separate occasions outside of our institution. Four months later, the patient presented with painless proptosis. After subsequent treatments, the patient presented with left-sided facial numbness seventeen months later.

Physical Examination:
Initial presentation showed a left upper eyelid mass. Later examinations revealed proptosis.

Diagnostic Tests:
- Histopathology: Revealed a multinodular proliferation of osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells and mononuclear cells demonstrating increased mitotic activity. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD68 and negative for CD45, S100, desmin, and lysozyme.- Imaging Studies:  Image Title: MRI of the orbits  Image Description: Axial T1-weighted fat-saturated postgadolinium MRI shows lesion with marked interval enlargement within the orbit and extension through the frontal sinus into the intracranial compartment  Image Title: MRI of the skull base  Image Description: Axial T1-weighted postgadolinium MRI shows tumor centered at the left cavernous sinus and orbital apex involving the left intracavernous/supraclinoid segments of the internal carotid artery with extension into the right cavernous sinus and right sphenoid sinus and with mass effect on the left temporal lobe- Genetic Testing: Next-generation sequencing of the tumor demonstrated a splicing variant (c.2515-1G>A) in the partner and localizer of BRCA2 (PALB2)
